segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Working together with him, we also appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “At a favorable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, now is the truly favorable time; look, now is the day of salvation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We give no cause for stumbling in anything, so that no fault may be found with our service,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but in everything we commend ourselves as God’s servants: in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in dire straits,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in hard labor, in sleepless nights, in hunger,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love without pretense,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in the word of truth, in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet true,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as unknown and yet well known, as dying, and look, we live; as disciplined and yet not put to death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as grieving yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have spoken openly to you, Corinthians; our heart is opened wide.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are not cramped for room in us; you are cramped in your own affections.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As a fair exchange—I speak as to children—open yourselves wide too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be yoked in a mismatched pair with unbelievers. For what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What harmony has Christ with Beliar, or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And what agreement has God’s temple with idols? For we are the temple of the living God, just as God said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will welcome you,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

notes.note: The Greek says only 'working together' and names no partner. Most translations supply 'with him' (God), because the previous sentence has God making his appeal through Paul, and that is followed here. The partner could instead be the Corinthians, or Paul's fellow workers.

notes.phrase: “At a favorable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.”
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form, where God addresses his Servant. In applying it, Paul replaces the quotation's word for 'favorable' with a stronger compound of the same word, rendered here 'truly favorable'.

The noun belongs to the same word-family as 'servants' in the next verse, and 'service' keeps that link visible. 'Ministry', the usual rendering, now suggests a clerical office, whereas the Greek word means carrying out a task on someone's behalf. The Greek says simply 'the service'; 'our' is supplied for English.

The word normally means fasting as a religious practice. In a list of hardships that includes beatings, prisons and sleepless nights, most interpreters take it as going without food from necessity. Voluntary fasting remains possible.

notes.traditional: by the Holy Ghost / the Holy Spirit
notes.note: The phrase stands without the article in a list of personal qualities, so some read it as 'in a spirit of holiness', a holy disposition. Most translations and commentators take it as the Holy Spirit, as here. The pairing with 'the power of God' in the next verse supports that reading.

The Greek can mean the message that is true, that is, the gospel, as the same phrase does elsewhere in the Pauline letters. It can also mean 'truthful speech', a quality of Paul's own conduct. Translations are divided; the pairing with 'the power of God' slightly favors the first.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God's action to set things right. Some scholars prefer 'justice' in English. Weapons 'for the right hand and the left' probably means a full kit, sword in the right hand for attack and shield in the left for defense.

notes.phrase: as disciplined and yet not put to death
notes.note: The wording echoes Psalm 118:18 (117:18 in the Greek numbering): 'The Lord disciplined me severely, but did not hand me over to death.' The preceding 'and look, we live' may echo the verse before it in the same psalm, 'I shall not die, but live.'

The verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It recalls the Torah's ban on pairing animals of different kinds (Leviticus 19:19 in Greek uses the related adjective; compare Deuteronomy 22:10 on ploughing with an ox and a donkey together). The point is difference of kind, not inequality of rank, which 'unequally' can suggest. Paul does not say which partnerships he has in mind; marriage, business ties and involvement in pagan worship have all been proposed.

The passage from here to 7:1 interrupts Paul's appeal for open hearts, which resumes at 7:2, and it contains several words found nowhere else in his letters. Some scholars therefore think it is a fragment from another letter or a later insertion. No manuscript omits it, and many scholars defend it as Paul's own digression.

Beliar is a variant form of Belial, from a Hebrew word meaning 'worthlessness'. In Jewish writings of the period, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, it is a name for the chief adversary of God. This is its only occurrence in the New Testament.

Many manuscripts read 'you are the temple of the living God'. The reading 'we are' has strong early support and is the more likely original. 'You are' probably arose under the influence of 1 Corinthians 3:16.

notes.phrase: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.
notes.note: Verses 16–18 weave several scriptural passages into one continuous quotation. They are Leviticus 26:11–12 with Ezekiel 37:27; Isaiah 52:11; Ezekiel 20:34 ('I will welcome you'); and 2 Samuel 7:14, widened to 'sons and daughters', perhaps under the influence of Isaiah 43:6. The wording is adapted freely, not cited exactly.
